thesis: AI helps reading when returning users to a shared source and preserving independent judgment.

ideas.statement: Label quotation, paraphrase and interpretation; the author did not answer.
Assistance and delegation differ; test independent ability and preserve unrequested otherness.

evidenceAndExamples.statement: A reader stops at a difficult sentence and asks a chatbot: “What does this term mean here?” They receive an explanation, request an example, and return to the text. In this scene, technology did not kill reading. It removed an obstacle. For someone reading a foreign language, entering a new field, or needing accessible reformulation, such help can be precious.

We can imagine even better uses. The system shows the relevant passage, distinguishes concept meanings, compares chapters, and asks readers how they would apply the distinction. When lacking information, it says so. When formulating its own interpretation, it does not present it as the author’s statement. When detecting a possible contradiction, it supplies both passages, not a mysterious verdict.

Here the interactive response fulfills one desire the critique of writing in Phaedrus exposed: we can question a text. But a crucial difference must remain. The historical text itself has not become a person, and the absent author has not answered. A system generated a response from information and rules. It can be useful without being confused with the author’s authentic voice. [ 1 ]

I would impose three simple labels on such an interlocutor: “quotation”, “paraphrase”, and “interpretation”. A quotation must be findable in the edition used. A paraphrase must preserve meaning without claiming verbal identity. Interpretation may go beyond wording but must state its basis. These are proposals for design and critical reading, not a description of guaranteed behavior in existing systems.
Imagine the following illustrative dialogue:
Reader: Does the author say people are selfish?
Assistant: In that passage, the author discusses a type of incentive, not whether all human motives are selfish. Here is the wording. Shall we examine the difference between the claims?
Reader: So I overgeneralized?
Assistant: That seems to be the problem with your interpretation. But let us also check the next chapter before drawing a conclusion about the whole book.

The dialogue’s value lies not in the system’s agreeableness but in sending readers back to the shared object. The text does not disappear into conversation. It becomes more accessible and easier to challenge. A good assistant can say “that does not follow” even when a more convenient conclusion would please its interlocutor.

Research on AI support for learning already exists but needs the same caution. An exploratory randomized study by the LearnLM and Eedi teams, published as a preprint in December 2025, involved 165 students from five British schools. The mathematics tutoring system was directly supervised by human tutors able to edit messages. Reported results favored supervised AI support; they do not demonstrate an autonomous chatbot’s equivalence to a teacher and do not concern literary reading. [ 18 ]

An artificial interlocutor can therefore do more than summarize. It can support questioning and practice if built and evaluated for these. But technical demonstration—the system can formulate a good question—must not be confused with educational demonstration—users learn better under well-defined conditions. The latter requires studies, comparisons, and relevant outcomes.

The librarian metaphor helps but has limits. A real librarian has a professional role, social relationship, and responsibilities. An automated system has behavior produced by architecture and a service. We can design it to support orientation without pretending every fluent answer represents care or human understanding. Respect for users begins with this honesty.

The most promising conversational book, in my view, is not one always sparing us reading. It knows when to answer directly and when to help us read better. A good dictionary does not destroy language. A good assistant should not destroy the encounter with text to demonstrate its usefulness.

Now imagine another evening. Readers request the book’s summary, then key ideas, objections, and replies to objections. Finally, the system produces a personal opinion “in their style”. In less time than the first chapter would take, they feel they have traversed the entire debate. What did they gain, and what did they not do?

For orientation, they may have gained much. We need not fully read every book about which we need information. The problem begins if we treat the conversational product as an experience we never had or competence we never checked. Knowing what someone might say in a discussion of a book is not identical to following its argument.

An exploratory study by Yue Fu and colleagues, in a preprint version revised in July 2026, followed 15 students’ AI use for course readings over eight weeks. The authors describe both comprehension support and strategies of triage and AI-mediated reading. The small sample and observational design permit no causal verdict about all students. But the study reveals the distinction between reading with assistance and delegating the encounter with text. [ 17 ]

Delegation is not automatically bad. In Evan Risko and Sam Gilbert’s analysis, “cognitive offloading” means using actions and external resources to reduce task demands. External tools can be useful, not merely weakening. The relevant question is what we delegate and what we must remain capable of doing. [ 16 ]

If I delegate finding the page, I can preserve energy for examining the argument. If I delegate examination, objection, and formulating my position too, what do I learn? The answer is not necessarily “nothing”: I can learn by reading the response. But I must check whether I can independently sustain the system’s distinctions. Otherwise, competence lies in the accessed service, not necessarily in me.

For some activities, reliable access to external competence suffices. We do not memorize every tool we use. For others, internal evaluative capacity is precisely what enables responsible assistance use. If I cannot recognize a mistaken interpretation, a personalized answer can become more convincing the better it matches my vocabulary.

There is another cultural risk: reducing otherness. A good book can ask questions I would not formulate. It can use an order I would not choose. If my access is limited to what I ask the system, I mainly encounter problems I already have language for. Personalization can open a work but also cut it to the outline of my ignorance. This is not technological fate; it is a design and usage choice.

An assistant can counter this risk by saying: “You asked about the conclusion, but chapter two raises a problem your question omits.” Or by proposing an uncomfortable passage, not merely one easily appreciated. Misunderstanding and disagreement must not automatically be treated as experiential defects to eliminate.

I would assess a book with a chatbot beyond immediate satisfaction. I would ask whether users can find passages, distinguish source from interpretation, formulate objections, and solve new tasks without assistance. For literature, I would also ask whether the system allows ambiguity or supplies a “correct meaning” for every sentence. These are proposed criteria requiring testing, not already demonstrated benefits.

The possibility of not conversing must also be protected. A text interrupting every page to ask how we felt has become a tiring guest. Sometimes the best interface is a visible button we need not press. Help must be able to wait.

The conversational book deserves to exist. But turning it merely into a device speaking ever better about works no one encounters would be a loss. A good future is not one where books answer every question for us. It is one where, after assistance, we have more questions of our own and greater ability to sustain them.

objectionsAndQualifications.statement: Small observational and supervised preprint studies do not establish autonomous literary benefits.

audit.notes: Complete chapter read; causal, geographical and methodological qualifications preserved.
